title: From Radio to Television
objective: After this level you can explain how American television borrowed its networks, shows and advertisers from radio.
summary: American TV borrowed radio's networks: NBC, CBS and ABC began in radio. Radio's stars, led by Milton Berle and CBS's 1948 talent raid, and its advertisers came along.

cards.headline: Early TV was called 'radio with pictures.'
cards.body: Television was first regarded by many as radio with pictures. In 1948 TV was still in its experimental stage, and radio remained the number one broadcast medium. So when television grew up, where did it get its networks, its stars and its money? From the medium it was about to overtake.

cards.headline: The networks came first
cards.body: NBC was formed in 1926. On November 15 that year, 25 radio stations in 21 cities carried its first network program from New York. Later the FCC refused licenses to companies running more than one network, so NBC had to sell its Blue radio network, which became ABC. Meanwhile NBC opened its first TV station in 1939, and by 1948 its TV network had 47 stations. TV's big networks were radio networks with cameras added.

cards.headline: Mr. Television
cards.body: Radio's biggest stars, such as Jack Benny, Bob Hope, and George Burns and Gracie Allen, were at first reluctant to risk their careers on TV. Milton Berle, who had had little success on radio, jumped in. His Texaco Star Theatre on NBC, from 1948, was TV's first hit and set off a dramatic rise in TV set sales. When it debuted, fewer than 2 percent of US homes had a set; by 1956, 70 percent did.

cards.headline: The talent raid
cards.body: CBS also began as a radio network, in the late 1920s, and grew under William S. Paley. In 1948 Paley signed radio stars away from NBC, including Jack Benny and George Burns and Gracie Allen. They proved as popular on TV as they had been on radio. The fight for television's future started as a fight over radio's stars.

cards.headline: Who paid for it all
cards.body: Advertising became the main way American broadcasting paid its bills: sponsored network programs brought money to both the network and its stations. Sponsors had a say, too. On NBC radio, breakout hits on the Blue network were often moved to the more popular Red network at sponsors' request. Television inherited the whole deal.

cards.headline: From radio: borrowed
learned: NBC, CBS and ABC all started in radio
Radio stars hesitated; Berle's 1948 hit sold TV sets
CBS raided NBC's radio stars in 1948
Advertisers paid for broadcasting, as on radio

questions.prompt: _____ became 'Mr. Television' with NBC's Texaco Star Theatre.

options.label: Jack Benny
options.rationale: Benny was one of the radio stars who hesitated at first.

options.label: Bob Hope
options.rationale: Hope was among the reluctant radio stars.

options.label: William S. Paley
options.rationale: Paley ran CBS; he didn't star in shows.

questions.explanation: Milton Berle, who had had little success on radio, starred in Texaco Star Theatre from 1948 and became Mr. Television.

questions.prompt: Match each name from early television with what goes with it.
questions.explanation: Milton Berle starred in Texaco Star Theatre, TV's first hit. CBS grew under William S. Paley, and NBC's Blue radio network was sold and became ABC.

questions.prompt: Level 1 dated General Electric's regular experimental TV broadcasts to 1928. Twenty years later, in 1948, what was America's number one broadcast medium?

options.label: Television, by a wide margin
options.rationale: In 1948 TV was still in its experimental stage.

options.label: Cable television
options.rationale: Cable was only just beginning in the late 1940s.

questions.explanation: Twenty years after GE's experiments, TV was still experimental and radio remained the number one broadcast medium.
